The Vestibular System

Touch reports contact. Proprioception reports your body. The vestibular system, deep in your inner ear, reports the motion of your head and which way is “up” — the sense that keeps you balanced and your vision steady.

Otoliths & semicircular canals The three vestibular reflexes Balance, gaze & life in space

Where we are

The third sense for action

This week’s unit has worked through the sensory systems that feed the closed-loop model from Lesson 1. Touch told you about contact with the world; proprioception told you about your own body’s position and movement.

The vestibular system adds a third channel: it senses the motion of your head and your orientation to gravity. It’s what tells you you’re tilting before you can see it, keeps your gaze locked on a target as your head moves, and triggers the fast adjustments that keep you from falling.

A close cousin of proprioception

The vestibular apparatus is so tied to body sense that Sherrington (1907) folded it into the proprioceptive system. We treat it on its own here because its receptors, reflexes, and research methods are distinct.

Feel it yourself

Fool your own vestibular system

Here’s a quick demo of the system you’re about to study. If you have an office chair that spins, try it (somewhere safe, with space around you):

  • 1Spin yourself around 8–10 times, then stop suddenly and hold still.
  • 2Notice that the world seems to keep spinning for a few seconds, even though you’ve stopped — and your eyes flick on their own.
Write & continue

You stopped, but your sense of spinning didn’t — and your balance felt off. What part of the vestibular system is responsible for this effect? Make your guess (or look it up) — and jot it down in a sentence or two.

Saved only in your browser, just for you. Jot something down, then continue.

You’ll see the answer on the semicircular-canals screen: the fluid in your canals kept moving after you stopped.

Overview

What the vestibular system is

The vestibular organs sit in the labyrinth — a set of fluid-filled bony tunnels in the inner ear, right next to the cochlea (your hearing organ). Each ear has one, and they come in two functional parts:

Two otolith organs

The utricle and saccule. They detect linear acceleration (speeding up, slowing down) and head tilts relative to gravity.

Three semicircular canals

Looped tubes set at right angles. They detect angular acceleration — rotation of the head — in all three planes of motion.

What it tells the brain

Together these give the CNS three things: self-motion, head position, and orientation to gravity and other inertial forces — the reference frame every other movement is built on.

What it does

The three vestibular reflexes

The vestibular system does its job largely through fast, automatic reflexes — and by telling self-generated motion (you turning your head) apart from externally imposed motion (a shove, a moving bus). Flip each card:

Flip for what each reflex does.

Signals travel from the otoliths and canals to the brain via the vestibular nerve (the vestibular branch of cranial nerve VIII).

Otolith organs · structure

How otolith organs work

Both the utricle and the saccule use the same clever trick: a layer of tiny crystals (otoconia — small calcium carbonate crystals) sits on top of sensory hair cells, and gravity or acceleration drags the crystals sideways, bending the hairs.

Acceleration or head tilt drags the dense otoconia sideways; the gel membrane shifts and bends the hair cells, which signal the brain.
  • •The macula is the sensory layer; it holds the hair cells.
  • •The hair cells project into the otolithic membrane, which carries otoconia — small calcium-carbonate crystals that are denser than the fluid around them.
  • •Because the crystals have mass, gravity and acceleration move them — and that movement bends the hairs.
Otolith organs · sensitivity

Utricle vs. saccule

The two otolith organs are oriented differently, so they pick up different directions of motion. Flip each card:

Flip for what each one detects.

An easy way to remember

Utricle → horizontal (think “you drive forward”). Saccule → vertical (think “sack dropping down”). Between them, the otoliths cover straight-line motion and tilt in every direction.

Semicircular canals · structure

How the canals sense rotation

Where the otoliths use crystals, the canals use fluid inertia. Each canal is a loop filled with fluid (endolymph). At the base of each sits a swelling — the ampulla — containing the sensory apparatus.

When the head rotates, the endolymph lags behind (inertia) and presses on the cupula, bending the hair cells in the crista.
Back to the spinning-chair demo

This is why the world “kept spinning” after you stopped: your head halted, but the endolymph kept moving for a few seconds, still deflecting the cupula — so your brain still sensed rotation.

Semicircular canals · the three planes

Three canals, three axes of rotation

Each ear has three canals set at roughly right angles, so between them they capture head rotation about all three axes. The three rotations have names you’ll see throughout motor control:

Pitch

Nodding up / down (“yes”).

Yaw

Turning left / right (“no”).

Roll

Tilting ear toward shoulder.

The canals detect angular acceleration in all three planes; the otoliths handle linear acceleration and tilt. Together they capture every way a head can move.

When vestibular signals go wrong

Vertigo: a false sense of motion

Vertigo is the sensation that you or your surroundings are moving, often spinning. Peripheral vertigo arises from a problem in the inner ear or vestibular nerve.

Common causes of peripheral vertigo

  • 1Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV): Displaced otoconia enter a semicircular canal. Changing head position can then trigger brief episodes of spinning.
  • 2Vestibular neuritis (neuronitis): Inflammation of the vestibular nerve disrupts balance signals and causes vertigo.
  • 3Ménière’s disease: Episodes of vertigo accompanied by hearing loss, tinnitus, and ear fullness; associated with abnormal inner-ear fluid regulation.
BPPV: useful crystals in the wrong place

Otoconia normally help the otolith organs sense acceleration and gravity. Inside a semicircular canal, loose crystals can disturb fluid movement and cupula deflection, creating a misleading rotation signal. Head injury can contribute, but BPPV can also develop without an obvious injury.

Think it through: why might rolling over in bed trigger BPPV?

The change in head position allows gravity to move the displaced crystals, stimulating the canal even after the head stops.

Sources: NIDCD: Balance Disorders; WebMD: Types of Vertigo.

Proprioception at the edge

The vestibular system in space

What happens to a gravity-sensing organ when there’s no gravity? Microgravity is a natural experiment that reveals just how much we lean on the vestibular system — and how well the brain adapts when it goes haywire.

  • •Astronauts can’t tell which way is “up” — the otoliths have no gravity to report.
  • •Many experience space motion sickness as vision and the vestibular signal disagree.
  • •After 24–48 hours, the brain effectively down-weights the vestibular system and relies more on vision and touch to move.
The unit’s big theme, one more time

Just like proprioception after a joint replacement, the motor system reweights the senses it can still trust. When one channel fails, the others take over — the central lesson of this whole week.

Unit wrap-up

Sensory-Based Control: the whole week

That completes the four senses that feed movement. Pulling the unit together:

  • 1We move best when the senses work together — touch, proprioception, vestibular, vision, and hearing.
  • 2Feedback and prediction both guide movement: feedback corrects errors; prediction (feedforward) lets us move quickly and smoothly.
  • 3Touch keeps us accurate, aids timing, calibrates grip force, and supports balance.
  • 4Proprioception tells us where our body parts are and how they’re moving — without it, fine control is very difficult.
  • 5The vestibular system keeps our balance, stabilizes our gaze when the head moves, and tells us which way is “up.”
The big picture

Good motor performance depends on combining information from all the senses. When one system is impaired, the others can help compensate — but only up to a point.
